planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Carlton is widely regarded as one of the very best daffodils for naturalizing and perennializing in the low-chill winters of the South, multiplying into large drifts over the years where many other daffodils decline.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Carlton bears large, soft yellow flowers with a slightly darker trumpet in a classic large-cup form, and has earned a reputation as one of the single best-performing daffodils for naturalizing across the South, reliably returning and multiplying into substantial drifts for decades with essentially no care, unlike many Northern-bred daffodils that dwindle after a year or two in mild-winter climates. Its fragrant flowers open in early to midspring and are excellent both left in the garden and cut for indoor arrangements. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom without braiding, tying, or cutting it, since the leaves recharge the bulb for next year's flowers, and divide congested clumps every several years after foliage yellows if bloom quality declines.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Bulbs for Texas

common_name: Grand Primo Daffodil (Classic Fragrant Southern Heirloom Tazetta)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Grand Primo is a classic Southern heirloom tazetta daffodil that has naturalized into huge drifts around old homesites and cemeteries across the Deep South for well over a century.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Grand Primo is one of the classic Southern heirloom pass-along daffodils, a multi-flowered tazetta bearing clusters of fragrant, creamy white flowers with a pale lemon-yellow cup on each stem, blooming reliably each winter in old Deep South gardens, cemeteries, and abandoned homesites where it has naturalized into vast drifts over a century or more with zero care. Its low chilling requirement makes it one of the most dependable daffodils for perennializing in mild Gulf South winters, unlike many modern trumpet daffodils that need cold most Southern gardens cannot provide. Allow the foliage to die back naturally without braiding or cutting it, and once established, simply leave the bulbs undisturbed to multiply on their own for years.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Bulbs for Texas

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Trevithian is a fragrant jonquil hybrid daffodil noted as a reliable perennializer in the low-chill winters of the South.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Trevithian bears one to two lightly ruffled, clear soft yellow flowers per stem with a rich, sweet jonquil fragrance, on a plant that reliably returns and multiplies year after year in Southern gardens where many Northern-bred daffodil cultivars fail to perennialize due to insufficient winter chill. Its jonquil parentage also gives it good heat tolerance and narrow, rush-like foliage typical of the group. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom without braiding or cutting it, since it recharges the bulb for next year's flowers, and leave established clumps undisturbed to naturalize over time.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Bulbs for Texas

common_name: Campernelle Jonquil (Classic Old Southern Heirloom Pass-Along Jonquil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Campernelle is one of the oldest and most cold- and heat-adaptable jonquils grown across the Gulf South, a classic pass-along heirloom bulb found at old homesites for generations.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Campernelle is an old hybrid jonquil, a cross between Narcissus jonquilla and a trumpet daffodil, producing fragrant, deep golden-yellow flowers on narrow, rush-like foliage, and has been passed hand to hand among Southern gardeners for so many generations that it is considered one of the truly essential heirloom pass-along bulbs of the region. Its exceptional adaptability to both cold winters and hot, humid summers has kept it thriving and multiplying at old homesites, cemeteries, and farmsteads across the Gulf South long after the people who planted it are gone. Allow foliage to die back naturally without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed, since Campernelle naturalizes readily and needs essentially no maintenance once planted.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Silver Chimes is a multi-flowered tazetta/triandrus hybrid daffodil that performs well and reblooms reliably in the mild winters typical of the Gulf South.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Silver Chimes bears clusters of three to six dainty, nodding, sweetly fragrant flowers per stem, white petals with a soft pale yellow cup, combining traits from its tazetta and triandrus parentage into a graceful, late-blooming daffodil well suited to mild-winter climates where it perennializes more reliably than many large trumpet daffodils bred for colder regions. Its multi-flowered habit and light, airy form make it a lovely addition to naturalized plantings as well as cut flower arrangements. Allow the foliage to die back naturally without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over the years.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Bulbs for Texas
